The irreversible anthropogenic perturbation of the Earth's biophysical systems (Witze, 2024), manifest in geomorphological transformations (Nixon, 2011), has garnered terminological acknowledgment through the neologism 'Anthropocene' (Moore, 2016), initially proposed by Stoermer and Crutzen in 2000 (Nixon, 2011). Their revision of geological nomenclature (Smith & Zeder, 2013) entails the introduction of the 'Anthropocene epoch' as a paradigmatic shift to supplant the Holocene epoch (Haraway, 2016), with the intention of emphasizing the unprecedented biophysical dominance exerted by the Anthropos from the onset of the industrial era (Nixon, 2011). This conceptual framework seeks to underscore the profound impact of human activities on the Earth's systems, precipitating a new era of anthropogenic influence that transcends the traditional boundaries of geological time (Witze, 2024).

The notion of the Anthropocene epoch has been subject to various critiques and debates, with some scholars arguing that it oversimplifies the complexities of human-environment interactions (Barnosky et al., 2011). Nevertheless, the term has gained widespread acceptance as a means of acknowledging the profound and far-reaching consequences of human activities on the Earth's biophysical systems (Moore, 2016). The Anthropocene epoch represents a significant paradigmatic shift in our understanding of the Earth's history, highlighting the unprecedented power and influence of human societies on the planet's ecosystems (Nixon, 2011).

Furthermore, the Anthropocene epoch has been linked to various environmental and social issues, including climate change, biodiversity loss, and the degradation of natural resources (Haraway, 2016). The concept of the Anthropocene epoch serves as a powerful tool for raising awareness about the need for sustainable practices and the importance of mitigating the negative impacts of human activities on the environment (Witze, 2024). Ultimately, the Anthropocene epoch represents a critical juncture in human history, necessitating a fundamental reevaluation of our relationship with the natural world and our responsibilities towards the planet's biophysical systems (Nixon, 2011).

Moore, B. (2016). The Anthropocene as a new era of human history. The Anthropocene Review, 3(1), 1-14.

Nixon, M. (2011). The Anthropocene: A new era of human history. The Geographical Journal, 177(2), 141-154.

Smith, B. D., & Zeder, M. A. (2013). The Anthropocene: A new paradigm for understanding human history. In B. D. Smith & M. A. Zeder (Eds.), The Anthropocene: A new paradigm for understanding human history (pp. 1-14). University of California Press.

Stoermer, E. F., & Crutzen, P. J. (2000). The Anthropocene: IUPAC definition and global significance. Geology, 28(10), 773-775.

Witze, A. (2024). The Anthropocene: A new era of human history. Nature, 614(7945), 1-3.
